question: Rewrite your draft to strip the institutional tone: root out passive voice, stilted vocabulary, indirect syntax, and weak verbs that drown your individual voice.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Journalese drowns individual voice in an institutional swamp of passive voice, stilted vocabulary, indirect syntax, and weak verbs.

question: Decide whether to use first person based on your mission, not habit — first person is not voice, and voice is not first person.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But ﬁ rst person is not voice, and voice is not ﬁ rst person.

question: Adopt a persona — a distinctive stance toward your material — and ask what kind of personality you want to bring to the page.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: By adopting a persona, the writer adopts a distinctive stance toward the material, bringing an identiﬁ able personality to bear on the subject.

question: Decide where you stand as narrator — far in the background letting facts speak, near the audience adding commentary, or in front keeping focus on yourself.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: position refers to where writers stand as they narrate the unfolding story.

question: Develop a consistent voice that readers come to expect, one that emerges as you mature, relax, and become comfortable with your literary self.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: most narrative writers develop a consistent voice that readers come to expect, one that emerges as writers mature, relax, and become more comfortable with their literary selves.

question: Match your level of diction to the subject — an author's level of diction is one of the prime markers of style.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: In the world of narrative writing, an author’s level of diction is one of the prime markers of his style.

question: Cut long introductory phrases and clauses that back into long, complicated sentences — they flag the institutional voice of journalese.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Long introductory phrases and clauses that back into long, complicated sentences immediately ﬂ ag the institutional voice we call journalese.

question: Space your figures of speech through the writing, dropping about one for every three paragraphs so readers never lose sight of the one ahead.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: you want to space the metaphors out without spreading them so far apart that readers lose sight of those ahead. About one ﬁ gure for every three paragraphs seems about right.

question: Hunt for the right metaphor during rewrite, not the rough draft, so puzzling over it doesn't interrupt getting through the first version.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: I’m more likely to ﬁ nd a ﬁ gure during rewrite, when puzzling over just the right metaphor doesn’t interrupt the struggle to get through the ﬁ rst version.

question: As you edit, stay alert for clichés and root out hackneyed expressions, replacing them with something fresh.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: As I edit, I stay alert for clichés, which signal opportunity for rooting out hackneyed expressions and replacing them with something fresh.

question: Read every piece of writing out loud in a firm, clear voice, hear the false notes, and cut verbiage and simplify syntax so it sounds like you.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The best thing any writer can do is to read every piece of writing out loud.

question: Relax and be yourself when you write — tension makes your words rigid and formal, submerging your true voice in stiffened formality.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But the ultimate secret to letting your voice sound on the page is simply to relax and be yourself.

question: Write fast and loose in the first draft rather than agonizing over every word — relaxed, fast writing sounds more like yourself and is easier.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A relaxed writer is a fast writer, and fast writers sound more like themselves.

question: Turn to the full range of figurative devices beyond metaphor and simile — allusion, word play, and personification.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A real stylist may turn to allusion (“his Alfred Hitchcock physique”) or word play (hot dog brands engaged in “grinding competition”) or personiﬁ cation.
